items.stem: "Negative reinforcement is the same as punishment." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Negative reinforcement increases a behaviour by removing an unpleasant stimulus; punishment decreases a behaviour.
items.markingKey: Negative reinforcement increases a behaviour by removing an unpleasant stimulus; punishment decreases a behaviour. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following was the aim of the study by Skinner (1938) on operant conditioning in the Skinner box?
options: To investigate whether a token economy could increase adaptive behaviour in long-stay psychiatric patients
To investigate whether fear can be classically conditioned in a human infant
To investigate how consequences shape voluntary behaviour
To investigate whether filmed models can reduce children's avoidance of dogs
items.answer: To investigate how consequences shape voluntary behaviour
items.markingKey: C. Skinner (1938) aimed to investigate how consequences shape voluntary behaviour.

items.stem: Which of the following was the aim of the study by Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961) on imitation of aggressive models?
options: To investigate whether children perform better with guidance from their mothers than alone
To investigate whether children imitate aggression shown by adult models
To investigate whether observing peer models increases children's self-efficacy and achievement in mathematics
To investigate whether filmed models can reduce children's avoidance of dogs
items.answer: To investigate whether children imitate aggression shown by adult models
items.markingKey: B. Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961) aimed to investigate whether children imitate aggression shown by adult models.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A method in which students take turns leading discussion using strategies such as questioning, summarising, clarifying and predicting"?
items.answer: reciprocal teaching
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of reciprocal teaching.

items.stem: Outline the findings of Ayllon and Azrin (1968) and explain one conclusion about operant conditioning applied to human behaviour that can be drawn from them.
items.answer: Findings: target behaviours increased sharply when tokens were given and fell when tokens were withdrawn. Link: these results are evidence about operant conditioning applied to human behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (target behaviours increased sharply when tokens were given and fell when tokens were withdrawn); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about operant conditioning applied to human behaviour (not just restating them).

items.stem: Outline the findings of Bandura and Menlove (1968) and explain one conclusion about social learning through symbolic modelling that can be drawn from them.
items.answer: Findings: children who watched the modelling films showed less avoidance and more approach to dogs, especially after seeing several models with several dogs. Link: these results are evidence about social learning through symbolic modelling.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (children who watched the modelling films showed less avoidance and more approach to dogs, especially after seeing several models with several dogs); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about social learning through symbolic modelling (not just restating them).

items.stem: Lars writes: "Scaffolding means doing the task for the learner." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Scaffolding gives just enough help for the learner to succeed and is withdrawn as they improve; doing the task for them prevents learning.
items.markingKey: Scaffolding gives just enough help for the learner to succeed and is withdrawn as they improve; doing the task for them prevents learning. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between negative reinforcement and punishment.
items.answer: Negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing something unpleasant; punishment decreases behaviour by adding something unpleasant or removing something pleasant.
items.markingKey: Negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing something unpleasant; punishment decreases behaviour by adding something unpleasant or removing something pleasant. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the findings of Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961) provide evidence about observational learning.
items.answer: Findings: children who saw the aggressive model imitated specific aggressive acts; boys showed more physical aggression. Link: these results are evidence about observational learning.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (children who saw the aggressive model imitated specific aggressive acts; boys showed more physical aggression); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about observational learning (not just restating them).

items.stem: Outline the findings of Freund (1990) and explain one conclusion about the zone of proximal development and guided learning that can be drawn from them.
items.answer: Findings: children who had worked with their mothers improved more; mothers adjusted their help, giving more guidance to younger children and on harder tasks. Link: these results are evidence about the zone of proximal development and guided learning.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (children who had worked with their mothers improved more; mothers adjusted their help, giving more guidance to younger children and on harder tasks); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about the zone of proximal development and guided learning (not just restating them).

items.stem: Describe the study by Watson and Rayner (1920) and explain what it shows about classical conditioning of emotional responses.
items.answer: Watson and Rayner (1920). Aim: to investigate whether fear can be classically conditioned in a human infant. Method: An 11-month-old infant was presented with a white rat paired with a loud noise from a steel bar struck behind his head; after several pairings, the rat was shown alone. Findings: Albert cried and tried to crawl away when shown the rat alone; the fear generalised to similar objects such as a rabbit and a fur coat Link: classical conditioning of emotional responses.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: Albert cried and tried to crawl away when shown the rat alone; the fear generalised to similar objects such as a rabbit and a fur coat); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to classical conditioning of emotional responses. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: A student claims: "Social learning theory says children copy everything they see." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Imitation depends on attention, retention, ability to reproduce and motivation; models that are similar, high-status or rewarded are more likely to be imitated.
items.markingKey: Imitation depends on attention, retention, ability to reproduce and motivation; models that are similar, high-status or rewarded are more likely to be imitated. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using an adaptive maths tutor app as an example, explain scaffolding in the ZPD.
items.answer: A maths app used in Bogotá gives a hint after one wrong answer, a worked step after two and fewer hints as accuracy improves. The app acts as an MKO providing contingent support that is reduced as competence grows
items.markingKey: Context (A maths app used in Bogotá gives a hint after one wrong answer, a worked step after two and fewer hints as accuracy improves.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to Skinner (1938), explain how research has investigated operant conditioning.
items.answer: Skinner (1938). Aim: to investigate how consequences shape voluntary behaviour. Method: Rats (and later pigeons) were placed in a box with a lever; pressing the lever delivered food (positive reinforcement) or switched off an electric current (negative reinforcement), under different schedules. Findings: reinforced behaviours increased in frequency, and partial (especially variable-ratio) schedules produced high, persistent response rates resistant to extinction Link: operant conditioning.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: reinforced behaviours increased in frequency, and partial (especially variable-ratio) schedules produced high, persistent response rates resistant to extinction); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to operant conditioning. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Using Bandura and Menlove (1968) as supporting evidence, explain social learning through symbolic modelling.
items.answer: Bandura and Menlove (1968). Aim: to investigate whether filmed models can reduce children's avoidance of dogs. Method: Children who were afraid of dogs watched films of a single child or several children interacting increasingly closely with dogs, or neutral films; approach behaviour was then tested. Findings: children who watched the modelling films showed less avoidance and more approach to dogs, especially after seeing several models with several dogs Link: social learning through symbolic modelling.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: children who watched the modelling films showed less avoidance and more approach to dogs, especially after seeing several models with several dogs); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to social learning through symbolic modelling. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: With reference to Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976), explain how research has investigated scaffolding.
items.answer: Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976). Aim: to investigate how adults support young children in problem solving. Method: A tutor helped 30 children aged 3-5 build a pyramid from interlocking wooden blocks; tutor interventions and children's progress were recorded. Findings: effective tutoring was contingent - more help after failure, less after success; six scaffolding functions were identified (e.g. recruitment, reduction in degrees of freedom, demonstration) Link: scaffolding.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: effective tutoring was contingent - more help after failure, less after success; six scaffolding functions were identified (e.g. recruitment, reduction in degrees of freedom, demonstration)); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to scaffolding. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Observational learning is the most effective way to learn in the classroom."
items.answer: Observational learning is powerful for skills and self-efficacy, but it works best combined with practice and feedback.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: peer models increase self-efficacy (Schunk and Hanson, 1985); fast acquisition of skills. Arguments against: some learning needs practice and feedback (retrieval practice); imitation without understanding; conditioning and cognitive strategies also important. Supported judgement: Observational learning is powerful for skills and self-efficacy, but it works best combined with practice and feedback.
